answer:
**Not the same day this autumn.** The US and the EU fall back a week apart.

- **US:** Sunday, **November 1, 2026**, at 2:00 a.m. local time. Under US law DST ends on the first Sunday of November. [3]
- **EU (and most of Europe):** Sunday, **October 25, 2026**, at 1:00 a.m. UTC / 3:00 a.m. in central European time. The EU changes on the last Sunday of March and the last Sunday of October. [1][2]

So this year Europe gains its extra hour about a week before the US. (Note: the EU date above is the standard last-Sunday-of-October rule; I couldn't fully read two of the sources — one was a snippet and the other returned an HTTP 403 — but it's consistent with the EU's longstanding rule.)

One nuance: the US rule is "first Sunday in November," the EU rule is "last Sunday in October," so the gap between them varies year to year — in 2026 it happens to be one week (Oct 25 vs. Nov 1).

No, not the same day in 2025.

**US:** DST ended **November 2, 2025** (first Sunday of November), clocks back 1 hour at 2:00 a.m. [1]
**EU:** DST ended **October 26, 2025** (last Sunday of October), clocks back 1 hour at 01:00 UTC. [3]

They differ because US uses "first Sunday in November," EU uses "last Sunday in October." A gap (or overlap) like 2025's happens when the first-Sunday-in-November lands more than 4 weeks after the last-Sunday-in-October. In most years the two dates fall within days of each other but not on the same day — they are actually on the same calendar week only in some years.

**2026:** US = Nov 1, 2026; EU = Oct 25, 2026. Still 7 days apart. [1]

EU: **Sunday, October 25, 2026**, at 1:00 a.m. UTC (last Sunday of October) — clocks go back one hour. [2]

answer:
**No, it's not the same day.**

- **US:** Clocks go back on **Sunday, November 1, 2026, at 2:00 a.m. local time** (first Sunday in November) [1][2].
- **EU:** Clocks go back on **Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 01:00 UTC** (last Sunday in October) [3].

So the EU switches back **one week earlier** than the US. The two dates only occasionally coincide (e.g., when the first Sunday of November falls on the same day as the last Sunday of October — rare).

Note: The US House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July 2026 (would make DST permanent), but it's still in the Senate and not law, so the November 1 fallback stands unless Congress acts [2].
